strengths: Addresses a genuinely understudied and practically important problem: the lack of per-prompt diversity in text-conditioned visual autoregressive (VAR) models, which prior VAR work has largely ignored in favor of image quality.

The proposed Scale-Travel latent refinement is a novel and well-motivated idea that exploits the intrinsic multi-scale structure of VAR (re-encoding an intermediate latent into coarse-scale token grids and resuming next-scale prediction), drawing a sensible analogy to time-travel in diffusion models while correctly noting the direct mechanism does not transfer.
The overall framework is training-free and inference-time only, making it directly applicable to existing VAR models without retraining or fine-tuning, which lowers the barrier to adoption.

Experiments are broad and reasonably thorough: two base VAR models (Infinity, Switti), two datasets (MS-COCO, MJHQ-30K), multiple complementary metrics for diversity (LPIPS-MPD, Vendi), quality (ImageReward, FID) and text alignment (GenEval, VQAScore), plus Pareto-front analysis.

The supplementary material is strong, including scheduler ablations, scale-travel parameter studies, temperature/top-p comparisons, prompt-rewriting comparison, and an explicit inference-time breakdown (~15-24% overhead).

The paper is clearly written, with informative figures (e.g., Fig. 1 and the qualitative comparisons) and pseudocode (Alg. 1-2) that make the method reproducible; hyperparameters for the main table are given.
The observation that early VAR scales already capture coarse layout/semantics is an insightful empirical finding that underpins the refinement strategy.
weaknesses: The core diversity mechanism (condition-annealing via noise injection into the text embedding / <SOS> token) is a direct port of CADS (Sadat et al.) from diffusion to VAR; the incremental novelty therefore rests mainly on Scale-Travel, which is a heuristic without strong theoretical grounding beyond analogy.

Scale-Travel is essentially a re-encode-and-resume heuristic; the paper does not provide a rigorous justification for why discarding re-encoded fine scales corrects artifacts, nor a principled criterion for choosing the rewind stage m and start scale l (these are selected empirically), which limits insight into when the method will generalize.

The quantitative gains are mixed: in Table 1, scale-travel actually reduces some diversity metrics (Vendi, LPIPS-MPD) relative to condition-annealing alone (e.g., Infinity Vendi 7.68 -> 6.07), so the headline 'Pareto frontier' is largely a quality-recovery story rather than a strict dominance claim; the Pareto-front advantage in Fig. 6 is presented visually without a single summarizing quantitative measure.

Evaluation is limited to two (relatively small) VAR models and standard benchmarks; no evaluation on newer/larger VAR variants or on downstream tasks that would exercise the diversity benefit (e.g., search/reranking, personalization), despite the introduction motivating diversity for test-time search.

Some claims are supported only by qualitative figures and could be strengthened with more rigorous statistics (e.g., variance across seeds, significance of the reported relative improvements such as +45.45% MPD).

The method introduces hyperparameters (k_min, k_max, start/target scales, noise schedules alpha/beta) that require tuning per model/dataset, and the paper does not fully quantify sensitivity in the main text.
Limitations are acknowledged (residual artifacts in ~6% of samples, slightly higher inference cost), but the societal/ethical implications of improved generative diversity are not discussed in depth.

strengths: Addresses a real and underexplored problem: the lack of per-prompt diversity in text-conditioned visual autoregressive (VAR) models. The paper correctly observes that this issue has been overlooked amid the community's focus on image quality, and the motivating Figure 1 makes the failure mode immediately visible.

The proposed Scale-Travel refinement is a genuinely novel and well-motivated contribution. It cleverly exploits the multi-scale nature of VAR to emulate the 'time-travel' mechanism of diffusion models, rewinding intermediate latents to a coarser scale and resuming generation to repair artifacts introduced by noise injection. The pseudocode (Fig. 4) is clean and the analogy to diffusion time-travel is explained clearly.

The method is training-free and inference-only, requiring no fine-tuning or retraining, and the reported overhead is modest (~15–24% inference time per Table E.1). This makes the contribution practically deployable on top of existing VAR models like Infinity and Switti.

The empirical evidence is strong and broad. Pareto fronts (Fig. 6) across two datasets (MS-COCO, MJHQ-30K) and two VAR backbones show DIVERSEVAR consistently defining the frontier, and Table 1 quantifies the gains (e.g., +45.45% LPIPS-MPD with only −11.48% ImageReward on Infinity). The supplementary ablations on schedulers, CFG weights, scale-travel parameters, temperature/top-p, text-alignment (GenEval, VQAScore), and prompt-rewriting are thorough and useful.

The paper is well-written and clearly organized. The framing of the two-stage 'diversify-then-refine' pipeline is intuitive, and the qualitative comparisons (Figs. 5, G.1–G.8) convincingly illustrate that Scale-Travel removes the artifacts caused by condition-annealing while preserving diversity.
weaknesses: Partial novelty: the diversity-enhancement components (CFG scheduling and condition-annealing via text-embedding/<SOS> noise injection) are direct adaptations of existing diffusion techniques (Kynkäänniemi et al., Sadat et al.). The paper acknowledges this, but it means the core technical novelty rests almost entirely on Scale-Travel, which itself is a heuristic analog rather than a principled derivation.

Scale-Travel is justified primarily by analogy to diffusion time-travel, and the underlying rationale (that early VAR scales capture coarse layout/semantics and can therefore serve as a clean surrogate for refinement) is supported mostly by qualitative visualization (Fig. A.1, Fig. A.2) rather than a formal argument. A more rigorous analysis of why the rewind works and when it can fail would strengthen the paper.

Evaluation of quality relies on automated metrics (ImageReward, FID). ImageReward is a learned proxy for human preference, and FID is known to be sensitive to reference-set and preprocessing choices; no human study or user preference evaluation is reported. Since the central claim is a diversity–quality trade-off, direct human assessment of the 'quality' axis would be valuable.

Only two VAR models (Infinity and Switti) are evaluated. Given the rapid growth of VAR variants, testing on a broader set (or at least discussing generalization to other next-scale models) would make the claims about 'VAR-based image generation' more convincing.

The paper reports that ~6% of the most diverse samples still exhibit visual artifacts even after Scale-Travel (Limitations section), and text-alignment slightly degrades (GenEval/VQAScore tables). These residual failures are acknowledged but not analyzed in depth—e.g., which prompts/scales trigger them and whether a targeted intervention is possible.

The hyperparameters of Scale-Travel (start scale l and target scale m) are tuned per model (l=8, m=3 for Infinity; l=8, m=4 for Switti), and the supplementary shows sensitivity to these choices. A more adaptive or automatic selection rule would improve the method's usability, and the current manual tuning is a practical limitation not fully addressed.

strengths: Addresses an under-explored and practically relevant problem: the lack of per-prompt diversity in text-conditioned next-scale visual autoregressive (VAR) models, which has been largely overlooked in prior work focused on quality.

Proposes a training-free, model-agnostic framework that requires no retraining or fine-tuning and only modest inference overhead (~15%), making it easy to deploy on existing VAR models such as Infinity and Switti.

The scale-travel idea is a creative and reasonably elegant adaptation of the multi-scale structure of VAR (reusing the multi-scale encoder) to refine noisy latents, drawing a sensible analogy to time-travel in diffusion models.

The supplementary provides a fairly thorough set of ablations (scheduler variants for CFG/condition-annealing, scale-travel parameters l and m, temperature and top-p sampling, text-alignment via GenEval/VQAScore, prompt-rewriting), which supports the empirical study beyond the main text.
Writing is generally clear, the motivation is well-articulated, and the extensive qualitative figures (G.1–G.8) help the reader judge the diversity/quality behavior.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The two diversity-enhancement strategies explored (CFG scheduling and condition-annealing via noise injection into text embedding/<SOS>) are direct transfers from diffusion models [28, 55]; the paper itself states these can be applied directly to VAR. The main novel component, scale-travel, is a heuristic that re-encodes an intermediate latent to a coarser scale and resumes generation, and the underlying observation that early scales capture coarse layout/semantics is already noted in prior work [26, 69]. There is little theoretical or mechanistic justification for why scale-travel removes artifacts.

Heuristic hyperparameters with unclear generality. The choices l=8 and m=3/4 are selected empirically on the two studied models; the paper does not explain how to set these for other VAR models with different numbers of scales, which limits the claimed generality of the approach.

Limited evaluation scope. Only two VAR models (Infinity, Switti), two datasets (MJHQ-30K, MS-COCO), and proxy metrics (LPIPS-MPD, Vendi, ImageReward, FID) are used. There is no human evaluation, the Pareto curves rely on only 100 prompts, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported, so the empirical evidence is not as strong as the claims suggest.

The 'new Pareto frontier' claim appears overstated. In Fig. 6, particularly for MS-COCO-Switti, the 'Ours' curve is not clearly dominant across the range relative to condition-annealing, and some panels show only marginal gains. The assertion that DIVERSEVAR 'consistently sets the Pareto frontier' is not convincingly supported by the plots.

Selective framing of Table 1. The headline '+45.45% LPIPS-MPD with minimal quality degradation (-11.48% ImageReward)' masks a noticeable drop in ImageReward (1.22→1.08 for Infinity; 1.11→0.93 for Switti). Moreover, the quantitative comparison is against each model's default setting rather than against the best competing diversity method matched at equal diversity, which weakens the quantitative conclusion.

LPIPS-MPD is a perceptual pairwise-distance proxy that can be inflated by artifacts, and the paper's own evidence shows condition-annealing raises it largely through artifacts. It is therefore unclear whether the diversity retained after scale-travel reflects meaningful semantic variation or residual artifact-induced spread; a semantic diversity metric (e.g., DINO/CLIP-based) would materially strengthen the case.

Directly relevant baselines are relegated to the supplementary (temperature scaling, top-p, prompt-rewriting). A main-text comparison against these simple diversity mechanisms at matched quality would make the contribution more convincing.

Generality is not demonstrated. Showing the method on a broader set of next-scale VAR variants (e.g., VAR, RandAR, and other recent models) would be needed to support the claim that the approach generalizes across VAR-based generation.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: the lack of per-prompt diversity in text-conditioned VAR models, which has been largely overlooked amid the focus on image quality.

Provides a systematic exploration of inference-time diversity-enhancement techniques for VAR, including CFG scheduling and condition-annealing, and identifies text-embedding noise injection as the strongest diversity lever.

Proposes Scale-Travel, a simple yet effective latent refinement method that exploits VAR's multi-scale structure by rolling back generation to a coarser scale and regenerating to repair artifacts while largely preserving diversity.
Extensive experiments span image and video generation, multiple VAR backbones (Infinity, Switti, InfinityStar), and multiple datasets/benchmarks, with informative Pareto front analysis.
Practical contribution: the method is training-free and model-agnostic, and detailed pseudocode/ablation studies support reproducibility. Limitations are explicitly discussed.
The supplementary material is thorough, covering scheduler choices, scale-travel parameters, prompt-rewriting comparisons, class-conditioned VAR, and video quality dimensions.
weaknesses: The overall approach is largely an adaptation of existing diffusion-based diversity techniques to VAR, with Scale-Travel being a relatively straightforward rollback/re-encoding strategy; the conceptual novelty is moderate.

The diversity-quality trade-off is improved but not eliminated: ImageReward and text-alignment scores still drop versus base VAR models, and the paper acknowledges visual artifacts in approximately 6% of generated samples.

The claim of no substantial computational overhead is somewhat overstated: Scale-Travel introduces roughly 15–24% inference-time overhead and requires per-model hyperparameter selection (e.g., rollback scales, noise schedules).

The evaluation relies on automated diversity and quality metrics (LPIPS-MPD, Vendi, FID, ImageReward, VBench) without human studies; perceptual diversity and prompt-specific usability are not directly validated.

Theoretical analysis is limited: the paper does not deeply explain why text-embedding noise is superior or precisely how Scale-Travel restores semantics, leaving the method mostly empirically motivated.

Comparison with fine-tuning-based diversity methods is not uniformly favorable; some baselines achieve higher diversity or lower FID in certain settings, so the advantage over learned approaches is not absolute.

strengths: Identifies and addresses an important, under-explored problem: lack of per-prompt diversity in text-conditioned VAR models, and provides the first systematic exploration of inference-time diversity techniques for VAR.

Proposes a simple, training-free framework DiverseVAR combining text-embedding noise injection with scale-travel, a novel scale-axis refinement that leverages VAR's multi-scale latent structure to repair artifacts while retaining diversity.

Extensive empirical validation on image (MJHQ-30K, MS-COCO) and video (VBench, VBench-2.0) generation, including Pareto-front analyses, multiple metrics, ablations, and comparisons to CFG scheduling, condition-annealing, prompt rewriting, and fine-tuning baselines.

Demonstrates robustness across CFG weights, temperatures, nucleus sampling, model scales, and resolutions; supplementary material provides algorithmic details, pseudocode, and extensive additional qualitative/quantitative results.
Writing is clear, the method is well motivated, and the work is well positioned within related autoregressive/VAR and diversity-enhancement literature.
weaknesses: The quality-diversity trade-off is improved but not eliminated: ImageReward drops by roughly 11-16% relative to baseline in main comparisons, so the claim of 'minimal quality degradation' is somewhat overstated; the method still sacrifices some fidelity for diversity.

Scale-travel applies the multi-scale encoder to potentially corrupted intermediate latents Z_l; there is limited theoretical justification that the re-encoded coarse tokens remain on the model's clean manifold or preserve the original condition, and success appears largely empirical.
Inference overhead is reported at about 15-25% (e.g., Infinity from 2.115s to 2.638s), which is not negligible for a training-free test-time method and may limit practical deployment.
Evaluation is restricted to two image VAR models and one video VAR model; no human study is provided, and text-alignment metrics show minor degradation, which should be discussed more thoroughly.

The core refinement is heuristic and depends on selected scale-travel hyperparameters (l, m); although ablations are included, generalizability to unseen VAR architectures and sampling schedules is not fully established.

strengths: The paper targets an underexplored problem: limited per-prompt diversity in text-conditioned VAR models, which is important for generative modeling.
The writing is clear and the proposed pipeline is described in a reproducible manner, with extensive experiments across image and video VAR models, multiple datasets, and diversity/quality metrics.
The ablation studies and supplementary material are substantial, covering different noise injectors, schedulers, scale-travel parameters, model sizes, and inference-time overhead.
Scale-travel is simple, training-free, and empirically improves the quality-diversity trade-off compared with naive condition-annealing in many reported settings.
The empirical comparisons with CFG scheduling, temperature/nucleus sampling, prompt rewriting, and fine-tuning baselines are useful for contextualizing the method.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the diversity-enhancement stage is largely adapted from existing diffusion techniques (CFG scheduling and CADS-style condition-annealing), and scale-travel is a straightforward re-encoding of an intermediate latent using VAR's existing multi-scale encoder, with no theoretical justification or guarantee.

The claim of 'minimal quality degradation' is not fully supported. For example, ImageReward drops from 1.22 to 1.08 on MJHQ-30K and text-alignment/color-attribution scores decrease, yet the paper does not provide human studies or statistical significance tests.

The method depends on several per-model hyperparameters (e.g., travel start scale l, target scale m, kmax, noise scale), which are chosen using the evaluation benchmarks. This raises concerns about overfitting and limits practical automatic applicability.
The overhead is reported as 15–24% slower inference, which contradicts the framing of 'without substantial computational overhead' and may be significant for large-scale or real-time use.
Video results appear to use augmented prompts in some cases, complicating claims about per-prompt diversity and making comparisons less direct.

Diversity metrics such as LPIPS-MPD and Vendi may not capture semantic or human-perceived diversity, and FID can conflate quality with diversity; stronger evaluation protocol would be needed to substantiate the claimed Pareto improvements.

The main paper omits some relevant comparisons to training-based diversity methods, leaving it unclear whether the test-time framework truly advances the state of the art beyond carefully tuned baselines.
